title: Nimony brings safe native compilation to Nim
excerpt: Nimony compiles Nim to native code with borrow checking, static contracts and no C toolchain needed.
body:
Nimony arrived on the Nim master branch with a single, surprising change: a fresh build of the language can emit native machine code without ever invoking a C compiler. Drop the `bin/` directory on `PATH`, run `nimony n`, and the resulting executable runs directly on x86_64, ARM64, ARM32, AVR or RISC-V.

The source page notes that the binary is “stand-alone” and that the runtime is hardened against heap exhaustion, turning an out-of-memory condition into a recoverable error instead of a crash. This post walks through the concrete benefits Nimony brings, native code generation, compile-time contracts, borrow checking, and a few other safety features, so readers can decide whether the new toolchain fits their next project.

## Native code generation without LLVM or GCC  

Nimony generates machine code itself, bypassing the LLVM and GCC back-ends that Nim 2 relies on. Because the compiler does not inherit the “undefined-behavior” assumptions baked into C toolchains, the produced binaries follow Nim’s semantics exactly. The build system is incremental and parallel, meaning that a change in one file triggers recompilation only of the affected modules while still taking advantage of multiple cores. The result is a fast edit-compile-fix cycle even for larger code bases.

The binary contains only the code written by the developer and the minimal runtime needed for the target architecture. No C standard library, no external linker flags. As the Nimony page explains, the runtime is “hardened against heap exhaustion,” so running out of memory raises a recoverable condition rather than crashing the process. This design makes deployment to constrained environments, microcontrollers, embedded Linux, or bare-metal RISC-V straightforward.

## Compile-time contracts eliminate out-of-bounds indexing  

Nimony introduces a static-contract feature that forces every array, `seq`, or string index to be provably in range at compile time. When a module enables `{.feature: "staticContracts".}`, the compiler checks each indexing operation against the known length of the container. If the proof fails, compilation stops with an error that points to the offending line. Because the check happens before code reaches the binary, there is no need for run-time bounds checks, shrinking the final executable.

The same contract syntax can express user-defined preconditions. For example:

```nim
proc takeFirstThree(s: seq[int]) {.staticContracts.} =
  assert s.len >= 3
  result = @[s[0], s[1], s[2]]
```

If a caller passes a shorter sequence, the compiler rejects the call during type checking. This approach removes an entire class of buffer-overrun bugs without adding overhead at run time.

## Borrow checking catches iterator footguns  

Nimony adds a borrow checker that tracks when a value is borrowed and forbids mutation of that path until the borrow ends. A classic Nim pitfall is mutating a `seq` while iterating over it; the mutation can trigger a reallocation that invalidates the iterator. Nimony catches this pattern at compile time:

```nim
proc grow(s: var seq[int]; use: int) = s.add use
var s = @[1, 2, 3]
for v in s:
  grow(s, v)  # compile-time error: `s` is borrowed during iteration
```

The error arises because the `for` loop borrows `s` for the duration of the iteration. The borrow checker enforces prefix exclusion: any path that is currently borrowed cannot be mutated, while unrelated fields remain mutable. The same rule applies to iterators, references, and other aliasing scenarios, turning a subtle runtime crash into a clear compile-time message.

## Additional safety-focused mechanisms  

Nimony’s design includes several mechanisms that reinforce correctness without requiring a second list.

Sum types are matched exhaustively, and variant objects no longer need a separate discriminator enum. Tags live in the `case` section, and pattern matching binds fields directly, for example:

```nim
type Expr = ref object
  case kind: enum
  of Lit: value: int
  of Add, Sub: left, right: Expr

proc eval(e: Expr): int =
  case e.kind
  of Lit: result = e.value
  of Add: result = eval(e.left) + eval(e.right)
  of Sub: result = eval(e.left) - eval(e.right)
```

The compiler verifies that every possible tag is handled, preventing missed cases.

Marking a proc as `passive` turns linear code into a state machine, which is handy for splitting game logic across frames or handling cooperative multitasking without explicit callbacks.

Plugins go far beyond macros. Because every stage of the pipeline reads and writes NIF (Nimony Interchange Format), a plugin can inspect, diff, or transform the output of any stage. This makes it possible to write custom validators that look for deadlocks, race conditions, or risky recursion, and to generate code that targets GPUs or FPGAs.

The standard library ships with what most applications need: linear-time regular expressions, a TLS 1.3 client, HTTP client and server, JSON handling, and a math library. All of these compile to native code without external dependencies, reinforcing the “single language for the full stack” claim.

## The takeaway  

Nimony replaces the traditional C-based back-end with a native code generator that produces lean, target-specific binaries. Static contracts turn out-of-bounds indexing into a compile-time guarantee, and the borrow checker eliminates a common class of iterator bugs.

Together with exhaustive sum-type matching, passive procs, and an extensible plugin system, Nimony offers a safer, more predictable development experience for projects that need both low-level control and high-level ergonomics. The next step is to try the master-branch build, add `{.feature: "staticContracts".}` to a module, and observe how the compiler catches errors that would otherwise surface at run time.
